title: Shuffle V2 in Ray Data: Faster, Fault-Tolerant Joins and Aggregations | Anyscale
gist: Anyscale rearchitected Ray Data's shuffle engine (V2): shuffle intermediates now live as spillable, lineage-tracked objects in Ray's object store instead of accumulating in long-lived aggregator actors' heaps, removing the dataset-must-fit-in-memory ceiling and enabling compression, operator fusion, and Arrow-native vectorized aggregation. On TPC-H SF1000, joins that V1 could not finish complete in ~320s and one groupby-heavy query improves 53x, positioning Ray Data as a more credible engine for terabyte-scale AI data pipelines (dedup, feature joins, batch inference post-processing).

themes.theme: Shuffle as the scaling bottleneck in AI data pipelines

insights.claim: Core AI data-pipeline operations — deduplicating billions of records, joining features/modalities/model outputs across sources, and per-group statistics for filtering and scoring — all reduce to shuffles, making shuffle the choke point of large-scale data prep for training and batch inference.
insights.speaker: You-Cheng Lin and Yuanzhuo Yang
insights.so_what: Whoever solves shuffle at scale owns a critical layer of the AI data-infrastructure stack; watch shuffle performance as a differentiator among data engines (Ray, Spark, Daft, etc.).
insights.locator: Whether the output is a training corpus

insights.claim: Shuffle is the one operation Ray Data cannot stream: groupby, join, and repartition require all rows sharing a key in one place, so per-worker memory scales linearly with dataset size (10x data means 10x memory in the shuffle worker), which is why jobs that run at 100 GB fail with OOMs at 1 TB.
insights.speaker: You-Cheng Lin and Yuanzhuo Yang
insights.so_what: Explains why data-infra vendors' scaling claims break at the shuffle stage; a useful diligence question for any distributed data engine.
insights.quote: Shuffle is where these pipelines fail, where the OOMs happen, and where a job that ran fine at 100 GB falls over at 1 TB.
insights.locator: Shuffle is the one operation Ray Data cannot stream

insights.claim: Ray Data's V1 shuffle accumulates partition state in long-lived aggregator actors' heaps, so for concatenating operations like joins and key-based repartitions the cluster must hold the entire dataset in actor memory at peak — a hard ceiling that reducing aggregations (sum/count/unique) partially escape but joins cannot.
insights.speaker: You-Cheng Lin and Yuanzhuo Yang
insights.so_what: Legacy Ray Data deployments doing large joins are structurally memory-bound; upgrading to V2 is the fix rather than adding RAM.
insights.locator: 1. A dataset cannot be larger than memory

insights.claim: In V1 a partition exists only inside the actor accumulating it with no lineage-tracked copy, so losing a single aggregator actor loses every partition it owned and the whole shuffle cannot recover — a fault-tolerance hole at exactly the scale where node failures become likely.
insights.speaker: You-Cheng Lin and Yuanzhuo Yang
insights.so_what: Fault tolerance, not just speed, is the reliability wedge for terabyte-scale jobs on spot/preemptible instances — a cost lever for AI data-prep economics.

insights.claim: V1 sizes its aggregator pool once from a sample of the first few input bundles and reserves num_aggregators x num_cpus for the entire shuffle, so skewed data breaks the sizing with no way to resize, and idle reserved CPUs starve other pipeline operators.
insights.speaker: You-Cheng Lin and Yuanzhuo Yang
insights.so_what: Static resource reservation is a general anti-pattern in distributed engines; elastic per-task scheduling is where the utilization (and cost) gains are.

insights.claim: Shuffle V2's single core decision — materializing shuffle intermediates as ordinary Arrow IPC objects in Ray's object store instead of an actor's heap — simultaneously delivers disk spilling (no RAM ceiling), lineage-based reconstruction of lost shards (fault tolerance), measured rather than estimated reducer sizing, and elastic resource use with no standing reservations.
insights.speaker: You-Cheng Lin and Yuanzhuo Yang
insights.so_what: One architectural choice fixing four failure modes at once is the kind of leverage that shifts competitive position; strengthens Anyscale's case as the AI-native alternative to Spark for data prep.
insights.quote: Shuffle V2 comes down to one decision: shuffle intermediates live in the object store instead of a long-lived actor's heap. Everything else follows from that.

insights.claim: Because V2's map and reduce are ordinary Ray tasks with a materialized boundary between them, the design admits optimizations the aggregator architecture could not express at all — input coalescing, shard compression, fusion across the shuffle boundary, and vectorized aggregation.
insights.speaker: You-Cheng Lin and Yuanzhuo Yang
insights.so_what: Architecture choices gate the optimization roadmap; V2's headroom compounds over releases while V1 was a dead end — expect further gains in subsequent Ray versions.

insights.claim: Compressing shuffle shards with zstd cut spilled bytes by 91% and runtime by 26% versus no compression on a TPC-H SF1000 inner join (lz4: 68% and 21%), because the CPU spent compressing is more than repaid by bytes kept out of the spill path.
insights.speaker: You-Cheng Lin and Yuanzhuo Yang
insights.so_what: Compression on the shuffle path is a near-free 20-25% runtime win at scale — a direct compute-cost reduction for data-heavy AI pipelines.
insights.quote: Compared with no compression, zstd cuts spilled bytes by 91% and runtime by 26%. lz4 spills more than zstd but still cuts spilled bytes by 68% and runtime by 21%.

insights.claim: Codec choice should follow the job's bottleneck: zstd when the shuffle is IO-bound (trades CPU for fewer bytes), lz4 when CPU-bound, and none when data is already compressed.
insights.speaker: You-Cheng Lin and Yuanzhuo Yang
insights.so_what: A reusable tuning heuristic for any shuffle-heavy distributed workload, not just Ray.

insights.claim: Replacing per-group Python iteration with Arrow's native columnar group-by on both map and reduce sides yields more than 30x improvement on aggregate_groups tests, with nine aggregations vectorized (Count, Sum, Min, Max, Mean, MissingValuePercentage, ZeroPercentage, Unique, CountDistinct).
insights.speaker: You-Cheng Lin and Yuanzhuo Yang
insights.so_what: Pushing work from Python loops into native columnar kernels remains the single biggest performance lever in Python data infrastructure — a recurring pattern (Arrow, Polars, DuckDB) worth tracking as a moat criterion.

insights.claim: Input coalescing buffers input blocks into 1 GiB (default) node-local map tasks because the shuffle otherwise creates map_tasks x partitions intermediate objects, whose count can grow until the head node itself OOMs from tracking them — object-count, not just byte volume, is a first-class scaling limit.
insights.speaker: You-Cheng Lin and Yuanzhuo Yang
insights.so_what: Metadata/control-plane scaling (driver tracking millions of object references) is an underappreciated failure mode in distributed systems diligence.

insights.claim: On TPC-H SF1000 (33-node AWS m5 cluster, Ray 2.58), query q21 went from 6,300 seconds on V1 to 2,400 on V2's architecture alone and to 119 seconds with vectorization — 53x end to end — while joins and map_groups that V1 could not finish at all now complete, with all four join types finishing in about 320 seconds.
insights.speaker: You-Cheng Lin and Yuanzhuo Yang
insights.so_what: Order-of-magnitude gains plus completing previously-impossible workloads materially expands Ray Data's addressable workloads versus Spark-class engines.

insights.claim: The authors disclose that V2's architecture alone is slower than V1 on queries where little data actually shuffles (q1: 361s vs 240s; q13/q15 similar) because the extra encode and object-store round trip outweigh the architectural savings — only with vectorization enabled does V2 win every query.
insights.speaker: You-Cheng Lin and Yuanzhuo Yang
insights.so_what: Rare vendor honesty about regressions raises credibility of the headline numbers; also a reminder that materialization architectures tax small-shuffle workloads.
insights.quote: That happens when little data really gets shuffled — a filter or projection upstream leaves the shuffle small, so V2's extra encode and object-store round trip cost more than the architecture saves.

insights.claim: The benchmark's timeout-marked V1 bars mean reported speedups for joins and map_groups are lower bounds computed against the timeout — the real gap versus V1 is larger than the numbers shown.
insights.speaker: You-Cheng Lin and Yuanzhuo Yang
insights.so_what: Understated rather than inflated benchmark framing; treat the join speedups as conservative.
insights.locator: Bars marked timeout did not finish

insights.claim: A forthcoming disk-shuffle mode (targeted for Ray 2.59) bypasses the object store entirely: one indexed file per mapper collapses object counts to one handle per mapper, and a per-node Arrow Flight server serves partition byte ranges — removing the driver's object-reference ceiling as the next scaling wall.
insights.speaker: You-Cheng Lin and Yuanzhuo Yang
insights.so_what: Signals convergence with Spark-style external shuffle services but on Arrow-native protocols; watch Ray 2.59 for the release.

insights.claim: Ray Data plans to deprecate V1 hash shuffle and both sort-based shuffle strategies once sort() and random_shuffle() move onto V2, consolidating five shuffle strategies down to just SHUFFLE_V2 and GPU_SHUFFLE; V2 is available behind ShuffleStrategy.HASH_SHUFFLE_V2 from Ray 2.58 and is renamed SHUFFLE_V2 in 2.59.
insights.speaker: You-Cheng Lin and Yuanzhuo Yang
insights.so_what: V2 becoming the default path means its performance profile will define Ray Data's competitiveness; the retained GPU_SHUFFLE strategy hints GPU-side shuffle stays a distinct bet.

insights.claim: An incremental join — building a hash table from one side and streaming the other through in batches, bounding memory to the build side plus one batch — is planned but blocked on Arrow 26.0.0 landing, showing Ray Data's roadmap is coupled to the Apache Arrow release cadence.
insights.speaker: You-Cheng Lin and Yuanzhuo Yang
insights.so_what: Arrow is becoming the load-bearing substrate of the Python data stack; upstream Arrow releases are a leading indicator for downstream engine capabilities.
